author: Dr. Sundar Subramani
title: ISO 9001:2015 to ISO 9001:2026: What Has Changed and What Will Challenge Organizations?
summary: The real challenge is not changing the documents. It is changing the way quality is managed.In fact, one of the most important messages from the revision is that the fundamental philosophy of ISO 9001 remains intact. Customer focus, the process approach, risk-based thinking, performance evaluation and continual improvement continue to form the foundation of the standard. body:
The release of ISO 9001:2026 marks an important point in the
evolution of quality management.

Published on 16 September 2026, ISO 9001:2026 replaces ISO
9001:2015. But organizations already operating an ISO 9001:2015 Quality
Management System should not interpret this as a requirement to start again.

In fact, one of the most important messages from the
revision is that the fundamental philosophy of ISO 9001 remains intact.
Customer focus, the process approach, risk-based thinking, performance
evaluation and continual improvement continue to form the foundation of the
standard. ISO itself describes the revision as a targeted update intended to
improve clarity, usability and relevance rather than introduce a fundamentally
new management system.

So, what has really changed?

More importantly, what will organizations struggle with when
they try to make the transition?

From a compliance system to a management system that
actually manages quality

For many organizations, ISO 9001 has gradually become
associated with procedures, forms, audits, corrective actions and certificates.

The 2026 revision provides an opportunity to ask a more
fundamental question:

Does our Quality Management System actually help us
manage the business better?

That question is particularly relevant because the strongest
changes in ISO 9001:2026 are not about creating more paperwork. They are about
leadership, organizational culture, strategic alignment, risks and
opportunities, and people's contribution to quality.

ISO identifies five particularly important areas in the 2026
edition:

These areas deserve particular attention during transition.

1. Clause 5.1: Leadership and commitment

From "management supports the QMS" to
"management owns the quality culture"

Leadership has always been an important part of ISO 9001.

The 2015 edition already required top management to
demonstrate leadership and commitment to the Quality Management System. The
2026 revision, however, places greater emphasis on what leadership means in
practice.

ISO specifically highlights quality culture, ethical
behaviour and active contribution to QMS effectiveness.

This creates an interesting challenge for organizations.

It is relatively easy to demonstrate that the Managing
Director attended a management review meeting.

It is much harder to demonstrate that leadership decisions
consistently reinforce quality.

For example:

The likely challenge

Many organizations have historically treated quality as the
responsibility of the Quality Manager.

The 2026 edition makes that approach increasingly difficult
to defend.

The Quality Manager can coordinate the QMS.

But top management must own it.

This may require organizations to change leadership
behaviours rather than simply revise procedures.

2. Clause 5.2: Quality policy

From a statement on the wall to a connection between
quality and strategy

The quality policy has often become one of the most
ceremonial elements of an ISO management system.

It is displayed on notice boards, included in induction
programmes and reviewed during audits.

But ask employees:

"How does the quality policy influence the decisions
your organization makes?"

The answer may be very different.

ISO 9001:2026 strengthens the relationship between the
quality policy, organizational context and strategic direction. ISO describes
this as a closer alignment between quality management and business strategy.

The implication is significant.

The quality policy should not exist separately from the
business strategy.

There should be a logical connection:

Business strategy → Quality policy → Quality objectives →
Processes → Performance → Improvement

The likely challenge

Organizations may discover that their quality objectives
have historically been selected because they are easy to measure rather than
because they are strategically important.

For example:

"Conduct 12 internal audits."

"Provide 10 training programmes."

"Close corrective actions within 30 days."

These may be useful activities, but they do not necessarily
demonstrate business improvement.

A more mature approach would ask:

What quality results are critical to achieving our
business strategy?

That could involve customer retention, process reliability,
delivery performance, product conformity, service effectiveness, supplier
performance or reduction of recurring failures.

3. Clause 6.1: Risks and opportunities

From identifying risks to making better decisions

Risk-based thinking was one of the major characteristics of
ISO 9001:2015.

The 2026 edition provides greater clarity around risks
and opportunities, with a stronger emphasis on proactively addressing both.
ISO specifically identifies this as one of the important changes in the new
edition.

There is an important distinction here.

Organizations are generally comfortable discussing risks:

"What could go wrong?"

But opportunities require another question:

"What could we do differently to achieve a better
result?"

This could involve:

The likely challenge

Many organizations maintain a risk register because the
procedure requires one.

The risk register may contain dozens of risks, but
management decisions may rarely refer to it.

That is the problem.

A useful risk-management system should influence decisions.

The transition therefore provides an opportunity to connect:

Risk → Control → Decision → Performance → Review

rather than:

Risk register → annual review → filing cabinet

4. Clause 7.3: Awareness

Knowing the quality policy is not the same as
understanding quality

This is potentially one of the most interesting changes for
organizations.

ISO 9001:2015 already required awareness of the quality
policy, relevant quality objectives, contribution to QMS effectiveness and
implications of nonconformity.

The 2026 revision places greater emphasis on people's
understanding of quality culture and ethical behaviour.

This shifts the conversation from:

"Have you attended the quality awareness
programme?"

to:

"How does your behaviour affect the quality of what we
deliver?"

That is a very different question.

The likely challenge

Organizations may need to rethink their awareness
programmes.

A PowerPoint presentation followed by an attendance sheet
may no longer provide convincing evidence of awareness.

Organizations should consider whether employees actually
understand:

This means that culture may need to be assessed through
behaviour, not attendance records.

5. Annex A: A useful addition, but not another set of
requirements

One of the new features of ISO 9001:2026 is Annex A.

ISO describes Annex A as explanatory information intended to
clarify concepts, terminology and the intent behind requirements.

This can be particularly useful for:

However, organizations should be careful.

Annex A should not become another compliance checklist.

There is a risk that organizations will read every
explanatory statement in Annex A as an additional mandatory requirement and
create new procedures to demonstrate compliance.

That would defeat the purpose.

The better approach is to use Annex A to understand why
the requirement exists and how it can be applied effectively.

What about the other clauses?

One of the most important messages for existing ISO
9001:2015-certified organizations is that they do not need to rebuild
their QMS from the beginning.

ISO states that the 2026 edition builds on the existing
framework and retains the fundamental principles of customer focus, process
approach, risk-based thinking and continual improvement.

Therefore, organizations should review rather than
automatically rewrite areas such as:

The question should be:

"Does our existing system meet the intent and
requirements of ISO 9001:2026 effectively?"

rather than:

"Which documents do we need to rewrite?"

The real challenges organizations are likely to face

1. Changing management behaviour

This could be the biggest challenge.

Changing a procedure is relatively easy.

Changing leadership behaviour is not.

If quality has traditionally been delegated to the Quality
Department, organizations will have to reconsider accountability.

2. Moving from compliance to effectiveness

Many QMSs are very good at demonstrating that something was
done.

Fewer are equally good at demonstrating that it worked.

For example:

Training completed is not the same as competence
demonstrated.

Corrective action closed is not the same as problem
prevented from recurring.

Internal audit completed is not the same as process
effectiveness evaluated.

Management review conducted is not the same as management
made meaningful decisions.

The 2026 transition provides an opportunity to close this
gap.

3. Making quality culture measurable

Culture is difficult to measure.

An organization may claim:

"We have a strong quality culture."

But how do we know?

Organizations may need to look at indicators such as:

The challenge is to convert the concept of culture from a
slogan into observable behaviour.

4. Integrating quality risk with business risk

Another common challenge will be the separation between the
Quality Management System and the organization's broader business-risk process.

In many companies:

Business risk belongs to management.

Quality risk belongs to the Quality Department.

That separation is not particularly helpful.

A mature QMS should make quality risks visible within
business decision-making.

5. Avoiding unnecessary documentation

Ironically, one of the biggest risks during transition is over-documentation.

When a new ISO edition appears, organizations often respond
by creating:

The result can be a larger QMS without a better QMS.

The better question is:

What information is genuinely needed to control the
process and demonstrate effectiveness?

ISO 9001:2026 is intended to improve usability, not create
bureaucracy.

A better way to approach the transition

Organizations should consider a five-stage approach.

1. Understand

Leadership and process owners should understand what has
changed and, equally importantly, what has not changed.

2. Assess

Conduct a gap assessment against the 2026 requirements.

Do not assess documents alone.

Assess the actual process.

3. Strengthen

Focus particularly on:

5.1 → Leadership

5.2 → Strategic alignment

6.1 → Risks and opportunities

7.3 → Awareness and quality culture

4. Demonstrate

Allow the revised system to operate and generate evidence.

This is important.

A revised procedure sitting in the document-control system
is not evidence of an effective QMS.

5. Verify

Conduct an internal audit and management review before the
transition audit.

The objective should be to determine:

"Are we actually operating in accordance with ISO
9001:2026, and is the system delivering the intended results?"

The transition should be viewed as an opportunity

Organizations certified to ISO 9001:2015 have until 30
September 2029 to complete their transition to ISO 9001:2026 under the
published transition arrangements.

That may appear to provide plenty of time.

But organizations should not wait until 2029.

The transition is an opportunity to revisit a more
fundamental question:

"Is our Quality Management System helping us run the
business better?"

If the answer is yes, the transition may require relatively
little disruption.

If the answer is no, ISO 9001:2026 provides a useful reason
to change.

The organizations that benefit most will probably not be
those that produce the largest number of revised documents.

They will be the organizations that use the revision to
strengthen:

Leadership.

Culture.

Decision-making.

Risk management.

People's competence and awareness.

Process performance.

Customer confidence.

Continual improvement.

That is perhaps the most important message of ISO 9001:2026.

The future of quality management is not about having more
documents.

It is about having better decisions, better
